name: Epsilon Indi B
kind: A pair of brown dwarfs orbiting the star Epsilon Indi

items.reason: This is the mission target itself: both ends lie on its measured path.

changes.method: Dots seen only in WISE 2010 are paired with dots seen only in SPHEREx at 4.6 µm, 8″ to 190″ apart and of similar brightness. Each pair is then checked against the target's path, Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD.
changes.not_checked: Asteroids and comets are not checked. An unconfirmed pair is not a discovery.

checks.text: Measured speed matches the catalogue: 4.72 vs 4.68″/yr (difference 0.7%)
2.4× brighter at 4–4.75 µm than in the 3.3 µm methane band: the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf (a normal star would be below 1×)
Steady brightness between May 2025 and Apr 2026 (-0.01 ± 0.08 mag)

facts.headline: About 83 km/s across the sky
facts.detail: That is 2.8 times the speed of Earth around the Sun. It is sideways speed only: motion toward or away from us does not show in images.

facts.headline: Crosses the width of the full Moon in about 380 years
facts.detail: A typical star in these images needs more than 100,000 years, which is why this one stands out in a flipbook.

facts.headline: 12.1 light-years away: one of the Sun's nearest neighbours
facts.detail: The light in these images left it about 12.1 years ago.

facts.headline: Cold enough to hold methane gas
facts.detail: Methane survives only in atmospheres below roughly 1,300 K, cooler than any true star. It absorbs light near 3.3 µm, which is why this object is 2.4× brighter at 4–4.75 µm.
facts.basis: SPHEREx flux at 4–4.75 µm ÷ flux at 3.3 µm

limits: Motion: an object must shift 2 SPHEREx pixels (12″) to count as moving. Over these 15.8 years that means faster than 0.78″ per year. Slower objects read as “no measurable motion”.
SPHEREx alone covers only 12 months here: by the same 2-pixel rule, enough only for motion faster than 13″ per year. The 2010 WISE image is what makes slower motion visible.
Brightness: compared at 3 SPHEREx visits only. A change between or outside those dates is not seen.
Solar System: the page checks against Gaia stars only. It does not check asteroids or comets, so a moving dot without a Gaia circle may be a known asteroid.
Crowding: one SPHEREx pixel is 6.15″ wide, so two close objects can blend into one dot and one spectrum.
